questions.topic: Cardinality formula for a union

questions.stem: Two customer lists overlap, and a coordinator needs the count of everyone appearing on at least one of them.

answer.exemplar: Count the union by adding the size of each list and then subtracting the size of the overlap, because the shared customers were counted once in each list and must appear only once in the total. For example, lists of eight and six with two customers in common give eight plus six minus two, that is twelve distinct customers. Subtracting nothing would report fourteen, which counts two people twice, and subtracting twice would lose them altogether.

questions.explanation: The union is everyone on at least one list, counting each person once. Shared customers are counted twice when the sizes are added, so subtract once.
questions.hint: Each shared customer must be counted once, not twice.

questions.topic: Cardinality formula for a three-set union
questions.learningObjective: explain why a three set union needs a triple overlap term
questions.stem: Three overlapping queues need one combined ticket count, and any ticket filed in more than one queue must be counted just once.

answer.exemplar: Combine the three queue sizes with inclusion and exclusion: add all three sizes, subtract each pairwise overlap once, then add the triple overlap once. A ticket in exactly two queues is added twice and subtracted once, so it ends up counted once. A ticket in all three queues is added three times and subtracted three times, so it would vanish, and adding the triple overlap back restores it to a single count. The pairwise terms must be subtracted before the triple term is added back.

questions.explanation: Adding the three sizes counts a shared ticket more than once, so pairwise overlaps are subtracted and the triple overlap added back. Each ticket then counts once.
questions.hint: Track what happens to a ticket in all three queues.
